SOURCE ESSAY:
The card of invitation—for which I have to confess that, like a true social climber, I had to some extent angled—came at last, stating that my visit would be expected on the following day at noon precisely, and that evening dress was to be worn. As I did not receive it until late at night, and as some medals had to be bought and a carriage and pair hired, I was busy enough after breakfast. The medals were for distribution afterwards among certain intimates, and the carriage and pair was to convey my friend and me to the reception, because we wished to enter at the gate of honour, and if you would do this you must have two horses. A single horse, and you are deposited at the inferior door and have a long walk.

It was to one of the most famous buildings in the world that we are going—possibly the most famous—and the horses' hoofs had a brave resonance (not wholly to be dissociated from thoughts of Dumas) as they clattered swiftly over the stones, beneath archways, past sentries, and through spacious and venerable courtyards, to the foot of the famous stairway. After ascending to an ante-room, where colossal guards scrutinised us and splendid lackeys took our hat, we were shown into the reception-room, in the doorway of which an elderly gentleman in black with a black bag was talking with such animation to a major-domo that we had to interrupt them in order to pass.

In this reception-room, an apartment of some splendour, in which we were to meet our host, sufficient guests had already assembled to occupy most of the wall space—for that is how we were placed, in four lines with our backs to the walls. There were about ninety in all, I calculated, of whom many were priests and nuns and many were women, the rest youths, a few girls, and a very few civilian men. It needed only the swiftest glance to discern that my friend and I were the only ones who had complied with the regulation about evening dress. This, naturally, greatly increased our comfort, since we became at once the cynosure (as the learned would say) of every eye. In the centre of the room was a little knot of officials, including four or five soldiers, all chatting in low tones and occasionally glancing through the door opposite that by which we had entered, which gave upon a long corridor. So for some twenty minutes we waited, nervous and whispering, when suddenly the officials stiffened, the soldiers hurriedly fetched their rifles from the far corner (a proceeding not without humour when one considers all things), and the whole ninety of us sank on our knees as a little quick, dark man, dressed in white, entered the room.

To be on one's knees, in evening dress, at twenty past twelve in the day, facing a row of people, across a vast expanse of carpet, similarly kneeling, and being also a little self-conscious and hungry, is not conducive to minute observation; but I was able to notice that our host was alert and bird-like in his movements and had a searching, shrewd, and very rapid and embracive glance. Beneath his cassock one caught sight of elaborate slippers, and he wore a large and magnificent emerald ring.

As he was late he got briskly to work. Each person had to be noticed individually, but some had brought a little problem on which advice was needed; others required solace for the absent and afflicted; most, like myself, had medals of the saints which were to be made more efficacious; and three or four of the priests were accompanied by far from negligible or indigent old lady parishioners, to whom such an event as this would be the more memorable and valuable if a little conversation could be added. Hence, there was work before our host; but he performed his task with noticeable discretion. To me, whom at last he reached, he said nothing; but my friend, who is of the old persuasion, put to him the case of a dying youth and obtained sufficient assurance to be comforted. And all the while I could see the elderly gentleman in black with the black bag glancing round the walls from the doorway—his function, as I afterwards learned, being that of a doctor intent upon restoring to consciousness those (and they are numerous) who swoon under the immensity of this ceremony.

Having come to the last of his visitors, our host retired to the middle of the room and delivered a short address on the meaning of his blessing and the importance of rectitude. He then blessed us once again, collectively, and was gone, and we struggled to a vertical position, the elderly ladies finding the assistance of their attendant priests more than useful in this process.

My knees, too, were very sore; but what did I care? I had seen Pope Benedict XV.

message.content:
The invitation, which I must admit I had somewhat maneuvered to secure, finally arrived, indicating that I was expected to visit the following day at precisely noon. It specified that evening attire was required. Since I received the card late at night, I found myself quite occupied after breakfast, needing to procure some medals and arrange for a carriage and pair. The medals were intended for distribution among a select few friends, while the carriage was necessary for my companion and me to arrive at the reception in style, as we aimed to enter through the gate of honor. Without two horses, one would have to disembark at a lesser entrance, leading to a rather lengthy walk.

Our destination was one of the most renowned structures globally, possibly the most illustrious of all. The rhythmic sound of the horses' hooves echoed as they galloped across the cobblestones, passing through grand archways, past sentries, and into expansive, historical courtyards, leading us to the base of the famous staircase. After making our way to an ante-room, we encountered towering guards who scrutinized our presence, while elegantly dressed attendants relieved us of our hats. We then entered the reception room, where an elderly gentleman dressed in black was animatedly conversing with a major-domo, requiring us to politely interrupt them for passage.

Inside the reception room, which exuded a certain grandeur, we found that enough guests had gathered to fill most of the wall space—this was how we were positioned, standing in four lines with our backs against the walls. I estimated around ninety attendees in total, among whom were numerous priests and nuns, a fair number of women, several young men, a few girls, and very few civilian males. A quick glance quickly revealed that my friend and I were the only ones adhering to the evening dress code. This distinction undoubtedly heightened our comfort level, as we instantly became the center of attention, or “cynosure,” to use a more scholarly term. In the center of the room, a small group of officials, including four or five soldiers, engaged in hushed conversations, casting occasional glances towards the opposite doorway that led to a long corridor. For about twenty minutes, we fidgeted and whispered in anticipation until the atmosphere abruptly shifted; the officials straightened, the soldiers hurriedly retrieved their rifles from a distant corner—an action that struck me as somewhat amusing given the circumstances—and all ninety of us fell to our knees as a small, quick, dark figure in white entered the room.

Kneeling in evening attire at twenty past noon, facing a row of similarly positioned individuals across a vast carpet, while feeling slightly self-conscious and somewhat peckish, did not lend itself to close observation. Yet, I managed to gather that our host exhibited an alertness akin to that of a bird, with a keen, rapid gaze that seemed to encompass everything. From beneath his cassock, the glint of elaborate slippers was visible, and he adorned a large, striking emerald ring.

Due to his tardiness, he wasted no time in getting down to business. Each guest required individual acknowledgment; some brought forth specific dilemmas needing advice, others sought comfort for those absent or afflicted, while most, like myself, had medals of saints they wished to make more potent. A handful of priests accompanied elderly parishioners, whose attendance at such an event would be significantly more enriching with a bit of personal interaction. Thus, our host had an arduous task ahead, yet he handled it with commendable discretion. When he finally reached me, he did not utter a word, but my friend, who belonged to the older tradition, raised the issue of a dying youth and received enough reassurance to bring him solace. Meanwhile, I noticed the elderly gentleman in black, carrying the black bag, was observing the room from the doorway; his role, as I would discover later, was that of a doctor intent on reviving those who fainted under the overwhelming nature of the ceremony.

Upon concluding his individual interactions, our host moved to the center of the room, delivering a brief address that emphasized the significance of his blessing and the importance of moral integrity. He then offered a collective blessing to all present and took his leave, prompting us to rise from our kneeling positions. The elderly ladies found the assistance of their accompanying priests particularly beneficial during this maneuver.

My knees, too, were quite sore from the prolonged kneeling, but in that moment, I felt little concern for my discomfort. I had just experienced a remarkable moment: I had been in the presence of Pope Benedict XV.
